items.followUp: Define the resultant of two forces acting on a body.

rubric.why: A resultant vector is defined by combining the vectors and describing the effect it represents.
rubric.description: Identifies it as the vector sum of two or more vectors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the resultant is the vector sum of two or more vectors.

rubric.why: The resultant represents the combined effect of the original vectors.
rubric.description: States that it produces the same combined effect as the original vectors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the single resultant has the same effect as the vectors acting together.

modelAnswer: The resultant vector is the single vector that represents the combined effect of two or more vectors.
It is equal to their vector sum.

items.followUp: Define gravitational field strength at a point.

rubric.why: This is the defining relationship for gravitational field strength.
rubric.description: Defines gravitational field strength as gravitational force per unit mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the force-per-unit-mass definition.

rubric.why: The unit follows from dividing force by mass.
rubric.description: Gives its unit as newton per kilogram.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct unit.

modelAnswer: Gravitational field strength at a point is the gravitational force acting per unit mass placed at that point.
Its SI unit is newton per kilogram (N/kg).

items.followUp: A book weighs 5 N. With what force does it attract the Earth?

rubric.why: The action and reaction forces have equal magnitudes; the apple's weight is 1 N.
rubric.description: Gives the magnitude of the force as 1 N.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the apple attracts the Earth with a force of 1 N.

rubric.why: Newton's third law says the forces act on different bodies in opposite directions.
rubric.description: Identifies the Earth as the body attracted and/or states that the force is opposite in direction to the Earth's force on the apple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the Earth and the equal-and-opposite direction relationship.

modelAnswer: The apple attracts the Earth with a force of 1 N.
This force is opposite in direction to the Earth's gravitational force on the apple, according to Newton's third law.

items.followUp: Define one watt in terms of work and time.

rubric.why: The joule is defined using a force of one newton.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the applied force is 1 N.

rubric.why: Work of one joule is done when that force moves an object one metre in its direction.
rubric.description: States that the object moves 1 m in the direction of the force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the 1 m displacement in the force's direction.

modelAnswer: One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.

items.followUp: Define mechanical energy and name one form of it.

rubric.why: Mechanical energy comprises kinetic and potential energy.
rubric.description: Identifies kinetic energy and/or potential energy as forms of mechanical energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming kinetic energy or potential energy.

rubric.why: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy; a suitable example demonstrates it.
rubric.description: Defines mechanical energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energy, or gives a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition or one valid example, such as a swinging pendulum.

modelAnswer: Mechanical energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of a body.
Example: A swinging pendulum has mechanical energy.

items.followUp: State Newton's second law of motion and derive the relation between force, mass and acceleration.

rubric.why: Newton's second law relates the applied force to the rate of change of momentum.
rubric.description: States that the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied force and occurs in its direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the law's statement, including the proportional relationship.

rubric.description: Writes force proportional to the rate of change of momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the proportionality in symbols or equivalent words.

rubric.why: Substituting momentum in terms of mass and velocity leads to the force-acceleration equation.
rubric.description: Uses momentum as mass times velocity (or its change for constant mass).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the momentum substitution.

rubric.why: For constant mass, the momentum-change rate equals mass times acceleration.
rubric.description: Derives the final equation F = ma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final equation.

modelAnswer: Newton's second law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of that force.
Therefore, F ∝ Δp/Δt.
Since p = mv, for a body of constant mass, Δp = m(v − u).
Thus, F ∝ m(v − u)/t = ma.
In SI units, the proportionality constant is 1, so F = ma.

items.followUp: State the two conditions of equilibrium for a body in a plane.

rubric.why: Translational equilibrium requires zero resultant force.
rubric.description: States the first condition: the resultant force on the body is zero.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating the condition clearly, including its equation or equivalent wording.

rubric.why: Rotational equilibrium requires the total clockwise and anticlockwise moments to balance.
rubric.description: States the second condition: the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating the moment condition clearly, including its equation or equivalent wording.

modelAnswer: First condition: The resultant force acting on a body must be zero (ΣF = 0).
This condition ensures that the body has no linear acceleration.
Second condition: The sum of the clockwise moments about any point must equal the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.
Thus, the resultant moment or torque must be zero (Στ = 0).

items.followUp: Estimate the age of a 15-year-old in seconds. Take one year as 365 days.

rubric.why: The conversion uses 365 days per year, 24 hours per day, 60 minutes per hour and 60 seconds per minute.
rubric.description: Sets up the conversion from years to seconds correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct multiplication or equivalent unit conversion.

rubric.why: This is the result of converting 20 years using 365 days per year.
rubric.description: Gives the estimated age in seconds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct answer with seconds as the unit.

modelAnswer: Given: age = 20 years; 1 year = 365 days; 1 day = 24 hours; 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1 minute = 60 seconds.
Formula: time in seconds = number of years × 365 × 24 × 60 × 60.
Substitution: t = 20 × 365 × 24 × 60 × 60 s.
